candidate_skills.canonical_definition: Rewrite operands into subtraction-ready equivalent forms, especially by creating common denominators and, where specified, by normalizing mixed-number or zero-part representations.
candidate_skills.alignment_notes: A's Equivalent-form setup combines common-denominator conversion with mixed-number and zero-part operand preparation. B splits this into Create common denominators and Convert mixed forms, so both B skills map here. C has a clean Common denominator conversion skill; C's mixed-number preparation is bundled with regrouping in C S02, which is mapped under post-subtraction resolution to avoid duplicating skill IDs.

candidate_skills.canonical_definition: Subtract already aligned fractional numerators and whole-number components, and assemble the component results when that assembly is included in the subtraction process.
candidate_skills.alignment_notes: B and C both use the name Subtract aligned parts for subtracting like-denominator fractional parts and corresponding whole-number parts. A splits this same operation across Subtract like fractions for numerator subtraction and Handle mixed parts for whole-number subtraction and result assembly.

candidate_skills.canonical_definition: Resolve post-subtraction or mixed-number boundary issues by borrowing one whole as a fractional unit when needed and simplifying or formatting the final result.
candidate_skills.alignment_notes: A isolates borrowing/regrouping as its own skill. B combines borrowing with simplification in Regroup and simplify. C splits the same broad resolution work across Mixed-number regrouping, which includes borrowing one whole as d/d, and Simplify final form, which covers reduction, zero fractions, and final formatting.

alignment_summary: The three experts largely agree on three broad phases: preparing operand forms, subtracting aligned components, and resolving regrouping or final-form issues. The main alignment challenge is granularity: A combines denominator and mixed-form setup, B separates setup but combines regrouping with simplification, and C combines mixed-form conversion with borrowing while separating final simplification. Each skill ID is mapped once to the closest broader shared concept.
